strengths: Well-motivated problem: Relation hallucinations (~40% of all hallucinations) are underexplored and the paper provides clear motivation with concrete examples
Training-free approach: No fine-tuning required, making it immediately practical for deployment to existing LVLMs
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with effective visualizations (Figures 1, 2, 4) that clearly illustrate both problem and solution
Comprehensive experimental validation: Thorough ablation studies, sensitivity analysis, cross-model evaluation, and attention visualization
Consistent improvements across models: Gains hold across different LVLM architectures (LLaVA, InstructBLIP), suggesting generalizability
Good ablation results: Each component meaningfully contributes (Enhancement -1.14%, Multi-perspective -3.68%, Interleaved -3.08%), showing synergistic effects
weaknesses: Modest empirical improvements with high computational cost: Only 1-2% absolute improvements while requiring 4x inference time overhead; cost-benefit trade-off is insufficient for practical deployment and inadequately discussed

Limited novelty: Method is straightforward combination of existing ideas (chain-of-thought + ICoT multimodal memory); design choices like five-question decomposition and masking strategy lack principled justification
Narrow evaluation scope: Only evaluated on relation-focused yes/no VQA tasks; missing assessment on broader vision-language tasks; only 7B-scale models tested

Significant hyperparameter sensitivity: Performance varies substantially with λ and k_max (Figure 3b); optimal values appear dataset-specific with limited guidance for new domains, raising generalization concerns
Fragile keyword extraction: Relies on spaCy NLP without robustness analysis for misidentified keywords; no failure case analysis provided

Unclear technical justifications: Attention modification (Eqs. 5-6), entropy-based k selection (Eq. 3), and confidence-based weighting lack principled explanations; answer generation process not clearly specified
Incomplete statistical analysis: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing reported; unclear if ~1-2% improvements are statistically meaningful
Limited baseline comparisons: Only compares to 2 recent methods; missing comparisons to other hallucination mitigation approaches and simpler alternatives
Missing detailed error analysis: No systematic breakdown of failure cases, performance by relation type, or investigation of when/why method helps or fails
Reproducibility concerns: No code release mentioned, many implementation details in appendix, hyperparameters appear tuned to specific datasets

strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing relation hallucinations, which account for ~40% of LVLM failures but receive limited attention
Intuitive and well-motivated three-component approach with clear decomposition of relations into subject-object-relation components
Training-free method that requires no fine-tuning, making it practical for deployment
Comprehensive ablation studies (Table 3a) effectively validate the contribution of each component (1.14%, 3.68%, 3.08% performance drops)
Demonstrates cross-model generalization across two different LVLM architectures (LLaVA and InstructBLIP)
Well-illustrated case studies with attention visualizations effectively demonstrate the mechanism and show qualitative improvements
Consistent improvements on two relation-focused benchmarks (MMRel and R-Bench)
weaknesses: Marginal empirical improvements relative to computational cost: 1.7% accuracy gain on MMRel (LLaVA-1.5), 0.62% on MMRel (InstructBLIP), only 0.18% on R-Bench (LLaVA-1.5), yet requires ~4x inference time—this critical limitation is relegated to the appendix rather than discussed prominently

Limited novelty: primarily applies existing chain-of-thought techniques to a specific domain; heavily builds on ICoT (Gao et al., 2025) without substantial innovation; the decomposition strategy, while sensible, is relatively straightforward and template-based

Narrow evaluation scope: only tested on Yes/No relation classification in VQA format; limited to three relation types (spatial, action, comparative); unclear generalization to open-ended VQA, image captioning, or other vision-language tasks

Acknowledged but unresolved spatial relation limitation: authors admit that 'spatial granularity of visual tokens often misaligns with real-world object boundaries,' yet defer this to future work despite spatial relations comprising ~30% of benchmarks

Insufficient experimental rigor: no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or error bars; baseline performance obtained via re-implementation rather than original code, raising fairness concerns; unclear if results averaged over multiple runs

Dependency on brittle preprocessing: relies on spaCy for keyword extraction with no analysis of robustness to extraction failures or alternative question phrasings; no ablation study of extraction quality impact

Fundamental technical limitation not adequately addressed: paper acknowledges that attention distributions 'may not fully capture the underlying reasoning process,' yet uses them as primary mechanism for visual grounding
Hyperparameter choices appear somewhat arbitrary (λ=5, kmax=20, n=3) and tuned on specific benchmarks with unclear generalization to new domains or models
Missing comparative analysis: no comparison with other chain-of-thought variants (Tree-of-Thought, Graph-of-Thought) or broader reasoning methodologies
Limited model coverage: only evaluated on 7B open-source models; unclear if improvements transfer to larger models (13B+) or closed-source systems (GPT-4V, Claude, Gemini)
Lack of failure analysis: no categorization of remaining hallucinations or discussion of when/why ChainMPQ fails; no error case studies

Unclear whether improvements reflect genuine reasoning enhancement or merely output constraint from multi-step questioning without validation that improved attention patterns correspond to improved reasoning
No statistical significance testing despite modest improvement margins; cannot determine if gains are statistically meaningful

strengths: Addresses an important but understudied problem (relation hallucinations, ~40% of all hallucinations in LVLMs) with clear motivation and practical relevance
Well-structured, intuitive methodology with three clearly motivated modules that are easy to understand and implement
Training-free approach is a significant practical advantage over methods requiring fine-tuning or preference optimization

Comprehensive evaluation on two relation-focused benchmarks (MMRel, R-Bench) with consistent improvements across two different LVLM architectures (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP), demonstrating good generalization
Thorough ablation studies clearly validate each component's contribution and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis is provided
Excellent qualitative analysis with attention map visualizations convincingly showing focused, task-relevant attention patterns before/after
Clear, well-written presentation with informative figures and case studies that effectively illustrate the method's reasoning process
Solid technical execution with proper algorithms, implementation details, and mathematical formulations
weaknesses: Modest empirical improvements (1.7-2.4% on MMRel, 0.18-2.21% on R-Bench) that, while consistent, are incremental rather than transformative for a top-tier venue

Significant 4x computational overhead during inference is mentioned only casually in the appendix and deserves more prominent discussion and cost-benefit analysis; this substantially limits practical deployment
Limited evaluation scope restricted to Yes/No binary VQA questions; no evaluation on open-ended relation reasoning or other downstream tasks
Only two 7B-parameter models tested; unclear if approach generalizes to larger models, different architectures, or models with fundamentally different attention mechanisms
Reliance on spaCy for keyword extraction without error analysis; no investigation of robustness when keywords are missed or misidentified
Several design choices lack clear justification: why 5 specific questions rather than other numbers, why cross-attention for enhancement, why this specific masking strategy
Confidence weighting parameter α in Eq. 5 is used but never explicitly defined, making reproducibility challenging
Limited baseline comparisons; only two prior methods tested; missing comparisons with other decomposition-based or chain-of-thought approaches
No systematic failure analysis or investigation of which relation types benefit most/least; paper acknowledges lower spatial performance but defers investigation
Moderate conceptual novelty; primary contribution is combining existing techniques (CoT decomposition, attention modification) rather than introducing fundamentally new methods
Incomplete reproducibility details: how exactly are V' used in subsequent questions, how are keyword tokens identified in Eq. 2, how is confidence computed
Hyperparameter sensitivity exists for λ and k_max with limited guidance for practitioners; claims of 'stability across models' based only on 2 models × 2 datasets

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored problem: relation hallucinations account for ~40% of LVLM hallucinations but receive less research attention than object/attribute hallucinations
Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 diverse LVLM architectures and 2 relation-focused benchmarks with proper ablations showing individual component contributions (1.14%, 3.68%, 3.08%)
Training-free approach that is broadly applicable without requiring model fine-tuning or parameter updates
Consistent cross-model improvements demonstrating good generalization across different architectural paradigms
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and case studies showing attention refinement and improved grounding
Strong precision gains on R-Bench (+4.17% with LLaVA-1.5) indicating reduced false positive relation predictions
Practical efficiency analysis with 'Light' variants offering better latency/accuracy trade-offs and sensitivity analysis of hyperparameters
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing concepts (Chain-of-Thought, cross-attention, attention propagation from ICoT) rather than introducing fundamentally new mechanisms; adaptation is relatively straightforward

Modest empirical improvements that do not justify computational cost: 1-2% improvements on MMRel, 1-4% on R-Bench while requiring 3.7× more inference time (3.3s vs 0.9s per sample); improvements diminish on stronger models (only +0.76% for InternVL3.5)

Critical methodological details are under-specified: confidence weighting (α_i) computation is not defined; entropy-based k selection lacks justification; bias mechanism interaction with softmax is unclear; hyperparameters appear fixed after limited tuning

External dependency on GPT-3.5 Turbo for question refinement introduces API reliance and potential failure points; no ablation studies on question quality impact or handling of NER extraction failures

Questionable core mechanism validation: paper acknowledges relying on 'attention distributions as a proxy for visual evidence' (Section 6) which may not capture true reasoning; no evidence distinguishing whether improvements come from genuine multi-step reasoning or simply multiple correction attempts

Limited evaluation scope: only Yes/No relational questions; no multi-hop relations or complex reasoning; minimal gains on general benchmarks (1-3% on MMBench, negligible on MME); missing cross-dataset generalization studies

Insufficient statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; no failure case analysis; type-specific performance (e.g., spatial category acknowledged as lower) not deeply analyzed
Reproducibility concerns: relies on external tools (spaCy, GPT-3.5); code not released; question refinement strategy may vary by model; implementation details scattered across appendix

Unclear generalization: performance improvements decrease on stronger models suggesting the method preferentially benefits weaker models; no analysis of whether learned patterns transfer to out-of-distribution relations

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Relation hallucinations account for ~40% of hallucinations but are underexplored compared to object/attribute hallucinations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 diverse LVLMs and 2 relation-focused benchmarks with consistent improvements and thorough ablations
Intuitive, human-inspired approach: Decomposing relational reasoning into localization and verification steps is sensible
Training-free method applicable to frozen models without requiring fine-tuning
Strong presentation with effective visualizations including case studies and attention map analysis showing reasoning progression
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The three components are straightforward combinations of existing techniques (cross-attention, CoT, ICoT); core insight of decomposing relations into 5 questions is intuitive but not novel

Modest empirical improvements without statistical significance testing: 0.18-2.2% gains on narrow benchmarks; improvements shrink to 0.6-1.6% on general reasoning benchmarks, suggesting limited utility beyond relation hallucinations
Significant unaddressed computational cost: 3.67x slower than baseline (3.3s vs 0.9s per sample), which substantially undermines practical value proposition
Narrow scope and limited generalizability: Evaluation restricted to Yes/No VQA on relations; no evaluation on open-ended questions or other multimodal reasoning tasks

Unresolved technical dependencies: Method relies on GPT-3.5 Turbo for question refinement and spaCy for extraction, undermining 'training-free' claim and raising reproducibility concerns; no robustness analysis for extraction failures

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: Paper demonstrates that improvements occur but provides limited analysis of why decomposition works or what systematic error patterns remain; spatial relation performance acknowledged as fundamentally limited

Methodological concerns: Arbitrary hyperparameter choices (kmax=10%, n=3 layers, λ=5); no cross-dataset generalization testing; no significance tests despite small margins; single runs without error bars

Incomplete comparisons: Does not evaluate against Wu et al. (2025b) Triplet Description method; general benchmark results (0.6-1.6% gains) suggest this is not specifically powerful for relation reasoning

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies relation hallucinations (~40% of all hallucinations) as an understudied issue deserving attention
Practical training-free approach: Immediately applicable to existing LVLMs without model retraining, enhancing real-world utility

Comprehensive and robust evaluation: Consistent improvements across 4 different model architectures and 2 relation-specific benchmarks, plus general reasoning benchmarks (MMBench, MME), demonstrating genuine generalization
Thorough experimental analysis: Complete ablations quantifying each component, hyperparameter sensitivity studies, efficiency variants with latency trade-offs, and effective attention visualizations
Consistent empirical results: Improvements hold across all tested configurations (1.7-2.16% on MMRel, 0.81-2.61% on R-Bench), suggesting robustness
Clear presentation and methodology: Well-structured paper with intuitive figures, logical flow, and accessible explanations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Method primarily combines existing techniques (standard cross-attention, straightforward question decomposition, direct application of ICoT). Each component is not novel; contribution is mainly in their combination for relation hallucinations

Modest improvements with significant computational overhead: ~1-2% accuracy gains paired with ~3.7x latency increase (0.9s → 3.3s). Trade-off may be prohibitive for deployment-sensitive applications. Gains diminish on stronger models (0.76% on InternVL3.5)

Scope limitations: Evaluation restricted to Yes/No relation questions; unclear generalization to open-ended reasoning. Dependency on spaCy keyword extraction; robustness to complex questions, ambiguous subjects/objects, and cross-lingual settings is unexplored. No cross-dataset generalization analysis

Unclear technical definitions: Equation 5 confidence weight (α_i = λ · Conf_prev) is poorly defined—how is confidence computed? Entropy-based k selection (Eq. 3) lacks principled justification; weighted bias aggregation (Eq. 6) could amplify early errors without explanation

External tool dependencies: Relies on spaCy NLP and GPT-3.5 Turbo for question refinement (mentioned in A.3), introducing additional dependencies and costs. No analysis of extraction failure rates or impact

Insufficient statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Baseline implementations are authors' recreations; small improvements could reflect implementation differences rather than method superiority. No multi-seed evaluation typical for stochastic models

Missing analyses: No failure case breakdown; paper mentions lower spatial category performance but provides no detailed analysis. Limited exploration of alternative decomposition strategies. No justification for design choices (exactly 5 questions, specific 3 masking patterns)

Reproducibility concerns: No code release mentioned. GPT-3.5 refinement is a key dependency but not prominently featured. Some critical details (n=3 for attention layers, hyperparameter choices) scattered across appendix
